passage:
In my first term, Mehak, a final-year student, lent me her old laptop and a folder of notes. I was so grateful I nearly cried. It felt like the kindest thing anyone had done since I left Nagpur.
By November it felt different. Mehak would ask, loudly in the canteen, "Anjali, did you use my notes for the quiz? What did you get?" She signed me up for her dance society without asking and said, "You'll come, na? After everything." Once she texted to ask why I'd been "offline all evening."
I started walking the long way round the canteen.
Compare that with Rosie aunty in the mess, who slipped me a flask of rasam when I had a cold and never mentioned it again. I still feel warm when I think of it. With Mehak, I mostly feel like I owe rent.

qa.q: What did Mehak lend the narrator in the first term?
qa.a: She lent her old laptop and a folder of notes.

qa.q: How did Anjali feel about Mehak's help by November?
qa.a: Anjali felt obliged and watched, as if owing rent, uncomfortable enough to walk the long way round the canteen.

qa.q: What small step could Anjali try with Mehak?
qa.a: Anjali could thank Mehak once more, offer to return the laptop, and say plainly that the dance society isn't for her.

qa.q: How does Rosie aunty's rasam differ for Anjali?
qa.a: Rosie aunty never mentioned it again, so the gift left Anjali feeling cared for and free rather than in debt.

grounding: Shows a student receiving help that slowly carries hidden expectations, leaving the narrator feeling obliged and watched, compared with a clean gift.

passage:
Counsellor's note, Girls' Hostel B, second week of March.
Pooja (19) came in quiet and kept her dupatta twisted in her hands. In January a senior, Madhuri, gave her a full set of second-hand textbooks and her old cycle. Pooja described it as "the best welcome." Since then, Madhuri has asked her to fetch her tiffin daily, to wait for her after late lectures, and last week told the corridor, "Pooja wouldn't even have books without me." Pooja said, "I can't say no to her. I'll look ungrateful." She has stopped going to the common room.
We talked about the difference between a gift and a loan with conditions. Pooja decided to thank Madhuri, return the cycle, and keep the books. I told the warden to watch for any teasing in the corridor and will see Pooja again on Friday.

qa.q: What did Madhuri tell the corridor last week?
qa.a: She said, 'Pooja wouldn't even have books without me.'

qa.q: What was Pooja feeling when she said she couldn't say no to Madhuri?
qa.a: Pooja felt trapped and afraid of looking ungrateful, with the gift now weighing on her instead of helping.

qa.q: What did the counsellor do next, and why might it help?
qa.a: They helped Pooja name the difference between a gift and a conditional loan, supported her plan, alerted the warden and booked a follow-up, so she isn't handling it alone.

qa.q: How might Madhuri see the situation?
qa.a: Madhuri may truly think she was kind and is owed some loyalty, without noticing that the demands make Pooja feel small.

grounding: Shows a student who received gifts slowly feeling obliged and watched as the giver attaches demands, and a counsellor helping her regain dignity.

passage:
Thursday night
Sumit paid for my canteen lunch again today. That's the sixth time. At first it felt sweet. The first day he just said, "My treat, you look tired," and I thought, what a nice boy.
Now he sits next to me every lunch. Today he asked where I was at eleven. I was in the library! Why am I explaining myself? Then he laughed and said, "Arre, relax, you owe me six lunches anyway." Everyone laughed. I didn't.
Tonight Jaya gave me her old jacket because my hostel room is freezing. She just said, "Keep it, it doesn't fit me," and went back to her phone. I'm wearing it now. It feels different. Nothing hangs off it.
Tomorrow I'm going to pay for my own lunch, and his too, and say thank you properly. 😕
Shalini

qa.q: How many times had Sumit paid for Shalini's lunch?
qa.a: Six times.

qa.q: What was Shalini feeling when Sumit said she owed him six lunches?
qa.a: Shalini felt uncomfortable and watched, as if the lunches had turned into a debt Sumit could use to check up on Shalini.

qa.q: What would you advise Shalini for tomorrow?
qa.a: The plan to pay and thank Sumit is fine; Shalini could also tell him calmly that being asked where Shalini has been is not okay.

qa.q: How is Jaya's jacket different for Shalini?
qa.a: Jaya gave it and moved on, so Shalini can simply enjoy it with nothing hanging off it.

grounding: Shows a student who slowly feels obliged and watched after repeated treats, contrasted with a gift given with no strings.

passage:
Supervisor's note, accounts floor, Wednesday.
Uma returned this week with her right arm in a sling after her fall. On Monday Jatin carried her files, fetched her lunch and set up the voice-typing tool. Each time Uma said, "Sorry, sorry, I'm so useless, you shouldn't have to." Jatin's smile got smaller each time, and by Monday evening he had stopped offering.
On Tuesday I mentioned to Uma, privately, that a simple thank you might land better than an apology. She looked surprised, then nodded.
Today Jatin brought her chai. Uma said, "Thank you, Jatin, that really helps." That's all. He grinned, sat down, and they sorted the invoices together for an hour. Two others offered to help her after that. I'll keep an eye on her workload until the sling is off.

qa.q: What happened to Uma's right arm?
qa.a: It was in a sling after her fall.

qa.q: What does Jatin's smile getting smaller suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Jatin felt discouraged and a bit awkward, as if his help was causing guilt instead of being welcome.

qa.q: What did the supervisor do next that helped?
qa.a: They quietly suggested to Uma, in private, that a simple thank you might land better than an apology, and kept an eye on her workload.

qa.q: How did Uma's plain thank-you affect Jatin?
qa.a: Jatin felt useful and pleased, grinning and working with her for an hour, and others felt free to help too.

grounding: Shows a person learning to accept help with a simple thank you, which lets the giver feel useful.

passage:
Sunday, the new flat.
Jasleen arrived at eight with her car, a toolbox and a huge pot of rajma. She carried boxes up three floors, fixed the curtain rod, and wouldn't let me pay for petrol.
Old me would have said sorry fifty times. "I'm so useless, you shouldn't have come, I owe you forever." I actually started to. Then I remembered last year, when I helped her move, and she kept apologising, and I felt like I'd done something wrong by helping.
So I stopped. When she handed me a bowl of rajma, I just said, "Thank you. This means a lot." She lit up like a little kid. We ate on the floor between boxes and she said, "See? This is nice." 😊
I feel lighter tonight. Owe her a rajma.
Reena

qa.q: What did Jasleen bring to the new flat?
qa.a: Her car, a toolbox and a huge pot of rajma.

qa.q: Why did Reena stop apologising?
qa.a: Reena remembered feeling as if she'd done something wrong when Jasleen kept apologising last year, and didn't want Jasleen to feel that same discomfort.

qa.q: What small step could Reena keep practising?
qa.a: Reena could keep answering help with a plain, warm thank-you and, later, offer help back when Jasleen needs it.

qa.q: How did Jasleen seem to feel when Reena simply said thank you?
qa.a: She lit up like a little kid, which suggests she felt happy and useful. 😊

grounding: Shows a person accepting a friend's help with a simple thank you instead of self-belittling apologies, letting the helper feel useful.

passage:
When my first nursing salary came in, I felt rich for about two days. Then the messages started. Appa's roof repair. My cousin Manjula's college fees. A friend's birthday trip. Amma's "small thing" that wasn't small.
I said yes to everything for four months. By the fifth, I was eating instant noodles at night and snapping at Manjula on the phone for no reason. I hated who I was becoming.
So I sat with Appa and was honest. I told him how much I could send home each month without going under, and that I'd help Manjula with fees but not the new phone she wanted. He was quiet, then said, "You're right, Sudha. We forget you have a life too."
I still give. I just don't resent it anymore.

qa.q: Whose college fees did the narrator help with?
qa.a: Manjula's college fees.

qa.q: What was Sudha feeling by the fifth month?
qa.a: Sudha felt worn out and resentful, snapping at Manjula for no reason and disliking the person Sudha was becoming.

qa.q: What would you advise someone in Sudha's position?
qa.a: Have an honest talk with family about what can be given without going under, and, if money worries grow, talk it through with a trusted adult or qualified adviser.

qa.q: How did Appa respond to Sudha's honesty?
qa.a: Appa was quiet, then admitted the family forgets Sudha has a life too, which suggests he felt a little guilty and understood.

grounding: Shows a young earner who supports family and a cousin but sets a sustainable limit so that giving stops turning into resentment.

passage:
Team lead's note, customer support, Hyderabad, end of quarter.
Dhruv has been in the team eight months and is the first to say yes to anything. He covers colleagues' night shifts, stays late to fix others' tickets, and I've seen him lend money to two people this month. Last week he was short with a customer for the first time, and Kalyani told me he'd skipped lunch four days running.
I asked him to coffee. He said, "If I say no, people will think I don't care." I asked what he could keep giving for a year without breaking. He thought hard and said: one extra shift a month, and help with tickets before six.
He told the team on Monday. Kalyani took over the extra nights. Today he laughed on a call, the first time in weeks. I'll check in with him again next month.

qa.q: How long has Dhruv been in the team?
qa.a: Eight months.

qa.q: What was Dhruv worried about if he said no?
qa.a: He was anxious that people would think he didn't care about them.

qa.q: What small step did the team lead suggest, and why did it help?
qa.a: They asked what Dhruv could keep giving for a year without breaking, which let him set his own limit instead of stopping giving altogether.

qa.q: How might Kalyani see the change?
qa.a: Kalyani had noticed him skipping lunch, so she is probably relieved and glad to share the extra nights.

grounding: Shows a young earner who gives time and help to everyone learning to set a limit so his generosity can last.

passage:
Friday, late.
Deepak called again. My younger brother needs his bike fixed, needs a new phone cover, needs "just a little" for a trip with his friends. Last month I paid his college exam fee, and I was proud to.
Tonight I said yes to the exam fee part of next term and no to the trip. My voice shook. He went silent, then said "fine" and hung up.
I sat on my bed and felt like the worst person in the family. Then I looked at my own list. Rent. My course. The dentist I've been putting off for a year.
If I keep saying yes to everything, one day I'll say no to everything, angrily. I'd rather say a small no now.
Still feel guilty. Also, strangely, lighter.
Suraj

qa.q: What did Suraj pay for last month?
qa.a: Suraj paid Deepak's college exam fee.

qa.q: How did Suraj feel after Deepak hung up?
qa.a: Suraj felt guilty, like the worst person in the family, and also strangely lighter.

qa.q: What could Suraj try next time Deepak asks?
qa.a: Suraj could explain calmly what help is possible and why, so Deepak understands the limit is about lasting, not about not caring.

qa.q: How might Deepak have felt when he heard no to the trip?
qa.a: Deepak was probably disappointed and a little hurt, going silent before saying 'fine' and hanging up.

grounding: Shows a young earner who keeps supporting a sibling's important needs but says no to extras so giving does not turn into resentment.

passage:
Last Thursday I did something small that felt enormous: I didn't take Ojas's call.
I'd spent that whole week holding people up. Monday, Ojas's fight with his dad. Tuesday, my lab partner's panic about marks. Wednesday, two hours on the stairs with a girl from my floor who'd just moved from Imphal and was homesick.
Thursday night the phone rang again and my whole body sank. I let it ring, then texted: "Can't tonight, I'm done in. Tomorrow after class?"
Then I sat there feeling like a monster. I kept rereading the text for hidden cruelty. There wasn't any.
Ojas sent back "no worries, bro." The next day he said he'd sorted most of it himself.
I think I felt guilty because saying yes is what I always do, not because saying no was wrong. I'm Pranav, by the way, and I'm still practising.

qa.q: Where had the girl on the narrator's floor moved from?
qa.a: She had just moved from Imphal.

qa.q: What was Pranav feeling after sending the text?
qa.a: Pranav felt guilty, like a monster, rereading the message for cruelty even though there was none.

qa.q: What small step could Pranav keep using?
qa.a: Pranav could keep offering a clear later time, like 'tomorrow after class,' when already drained, instead of taking every call.

grounding: Shows a student feeling guilty for declining one call after a week of listening, and recognising the guilt as a habit of over-giving.

passage:
I'm the eldest daughter, which in our house means I'm the one who remembers everything. Tanvir's school fees, Ammi's blood-pressure appointments, Nana's birthday, the gas cylinder.
Last Eid I cooked for twenty people after a week of night shifts at the call centre. Everyone praised the biryani. Nobody asked how I was. At eleven that night I washed the big pots alone and cried into the sink, quietly so Ammi wouldn't hear.

Since her father's illness last year she has managed the household bills, her brother Kishore's college applications and her mother's hospital visits, while working full-time. Together we listed the tasks and marked which ones Kishore, now nineteen, could take over. She agreed to talk to him this weekend. I gave her the service's number for evenings and booked a follow-up for next Tuesday.

passage: In the staff room of Ward 6, Pallavi watched Jatin slam his locker. For two years he had been the nurse everyone called: swap my shift, cover my break, help me with the drip. Today he'd told a junior, "Can't you do anything yourself?" and walked off. Pallavi had never heard him say anything like that. She noticed his lunch box, untouched since morning, and the dark circles he'd been wearing for weeks. When he came back to fill his water bottle, she didn't lecture him. "Jatin, give me your two night shifts next week. I owe you about fifty." He frowned. "I'm fine." "You just shouted at Ruchi." He sat down heavily. "I haven't had a full day off in five weeks." Pallavi took out the roster and a pen right there.

qa.a: Five weeks.

qa.q: What was Pallavi thinking when she noticed Jatin's untouched lunch box?
qa.a: She seemed worried and concerned, reading his dark circles and snapping as signs he was worn out rather than just rude.

qa.q: How did Pallavi offer help in a way Jatin could accept?
qa.a: She skipped the lecture and made a specific offer, taking his night shifts, framed as paying back what she owed.

qa.q: What is it like for Jatin to be offered help after two years of helping?
qa.a: He resists at first, saying he is fine, then sits down heavily, which suggests he felt exhausted and relieved.

passage:
Dear Arnab,

I'm writing because every time I try to say this in person, you change the subject to someone else's problem.

You've been different these last few weeks. Short with the kids at the tuition centre. Leaving the group chat on "seen." Last Sunday you didn't come to cricket for the first time in three years. I know you've been driving your uncle to dialysis twice a week and covering the centre's accounts since Ravi left.

You're the one who always turns up for everyone. I don't think anyone has turned up for you.

So here's my offer. I'll take the Saturday batch for the next month. And on Wednesday I'm coming over with food, and you don't have to host. You can just eat.

Your friend,
Sudha

qa.q: How often has Arnab been driving an uncle to dialysis?
qa.a: Twice a week.

qa.q: What does Sudha seem to feel about the changes in Arnab?
qa.a: Sudha seems worried and caring, reading Arnab's curtness and absence as signs of being worn out rather than unfriendly.

qa.q: What small step does Sudha offer, and why is it well chosen?
qa.a: Taking the Saturday batch and bringing food with no hosting expected gives Arnab real rest without anything to manage.

qa.q: How might Arnab feel reading the letter?
qa.a: Arnab may feel exposed at first, then relieved and cared for, since no one has turned up for Arnab in a long time.

grounding: Shows a friend noticing that a usual giver has become curt and withdrawn and offering to help for a change.

passage:
"You look like I looked at twenty-five, Nikita," said Amandeep Bua, pouring out two cups of chai. "Let me tell you something. I was head of the school canteen committee, the temple accounts, my brother's children every evening. I said yes to all of it and thought that was goodness. One monsoon I fell asleep standing up in the temple store room. Truly. Mataji found me leaning on a rice sack.
The next week I did three things. I took Sunday afternoons for myself, no matter what. I gave the temple accounts to Sardar ji's son, who was dying to be asked. And when the canteen wanted me for a fourth year, I said no.
Everyone was upset for a month. Then they managed. And I was kind again, not just busy. That's the part I want you to remember."

qa.q: Where did Amandeep Bua fall asleep standing up?
qa.a: In the temple store room, leaning on a rice sack.

qa.q: How did Amandeep Bua feel before making the changes?
qa.a: Amandeep Bua was exhausted and stretched thin, saying yes to everything and mistaking that for goodness.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Bua's story, and what changed after it?
qa.a: Falling asleep in the store room; after that, Bua kept Sunday afternoons free, handed the temple accounts on, and said no to a fourth canteen year.

qa.q: How might Sardar ji's son have felt when given the temple accounts?
qa.a: He was dying to be asked, so he probably felt pleased and trusted.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling how scheduling rest, sharing the load and saying a clear no kept her kindness sustainable.

passage: The monsoon week hit Gurleen's school hard: two teachers down with fever, power cuts every afternoon, and a parents' meeting on Friday. Gurleen, the one who always said yes, had three extra classes, a play to rehearse and a colleague's report cards to finish. By Wednesday she was eating lunch standing up. That night, by candlelight, she made a list and crossed out three things. On Thursday she asked Charu, "Can you run the play rehearsal? I'll do your Friday duty next week." Charu grinned: "I've been wanting to direct for years." When the head asked her to take a fourth extra class, Gurleen said, "Not this week, Ma'am. I can do Monday." She went home at five on Thursday and slept for ten hours. On Friday she met every parent with a clear head.

qa.q: What did Gurleen ask Charu to do?
qa.a: To run the play rehearsal.

qa.q: What was Gurleen feeling by Wednesday?
qa.a: She was overwhelmed and worn out, eating lunch standing up with three extra classes and more work piling on.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Sharing the rehearsal with Charu and saying 'not this week' to the head worked, because she still helped but kept enough energy for the parents' meeting.

qa.q: How did Charu see being asked to take over the rehearsal?
qa.a: Charu was delighted, since she had been wanting to direct for years.

grounding: Shows a teacher who gives a lot sharing the load, saying a clear no and resting, so her kindness stays sustainable for everyone.

passage: Yogesh was the person the whole Pune office called when a laptop froze, and the person his whole family called when a phone did anything strange. He fixed Afreen's printer, his aunt's TV, his cousin's router, and answered messages till midnight. Last month he forgot his own sister's school play because he was on a video call with a neighbour's modem. That did it. He made three changes. Sundays became phone-off days, and he told everyone. He spent two lunch breaks teaching Afreen the ten most common fixes, and she happily became the office's second helper. And when a colleague asked him to set up a home network on a Saturday, he said, "I can't this weekend, sorry. Here's a guide." Two weeks later his sister caught him laughing on the sofa on a Sunday. "You're back," she said.

qa.q: Whose school play did Yogesh forget?
qa.a: His own sister's school play.

qa.q: What might Yogesh have felt after missing his sister's play?
qa.a: He probably felt guilty and disappointed in himself, which pushed him to change how he gave his time.

qa.q: What would you advise someone who is always the helper, like Yogesh?
qa.a: Choose one rest day, teach someone else the common tasks, and say a clear, kind no with an alternative when stretched.

qa.q: How does Yogesh's sister see the change?
qa.a: She is happy and relieved to have him back, noticing him laughing on a Sunday.

grounding: Shows a generous helper scheduling rest, sharing the load and saying no to some requests so his kindness can last.

passage:
After Nani died, I had a lot of questions. I asked Chandrika didi, my cousin, because she's in college and knows things.
"Why do people die?"
She didn't say "don't think about it." She said, "Bodies get old and tired, like Nani's did, and one day they stop working."
"Where did Nani go?"
"Different people believe different things. Some believe in heaven, some believe we come back. I'm not sure. I think she's in all the things she taught us."
"Why are we even here, then?"
Chandrika didi laughed a little. "Big question, Alka. I think maybe to love people and learn stuff."
I liked that she said "I'm not sure." It made me feel she was telling me the truth. That night I made Nani's lemon rice with Mummy.

qa.q: Who did Alka ask about why people die?
qa.a: Chandrika didi, Alka's cousin in college.

qa.q: Why did Alka like that Chandrika didi said 'I'm not sure'?
qa.a: It made Alka feel the answers were the truth, which seemed to comfort Alka more than a neat answer would have.

qa.q: How could a grown-up answer a child's big questions like these?
qa.a: Like Chandrika didi, they could give simple, honest answers, share different beliefs, and admit when they don't know.

qa.q: What would change if Chandrika didi had said 'don't think about it'?
qa.a: Alka might have felt confused and alone with the questions, and less able to grieve for Nani openly.

grounding: Shows a child asking why people die and why we are here, and being respected with simple honest answers instead of deflection.

passage:
Class 3 note, Thursday.
This morning we found Bubbles, our class fish, floating at the top of the tank. Most of the children were sad for a few minutes, then went back to drawing. Sumit (8) stayed by the tank. He asked me, "Why do things die? Will Bubbles be sad now? Where does a fish go?" Arnab, next to him, said, "Don't be silly, it's just a fish."
I didn't brush it off. I told Sumit that all living things have a life that ends, that Bubbles can't feel sad anymore, and that people believe different things about what happens after. He listened carefully and asked, "Will you die?" I said, "One day, when I'm very old, I hope."
We buried Bubbles in the garden at lunch. I've told his mother at pickup so she can continue the conversation at home.

qa.q: What was the class fish called?
qa.a: Bubbles.

qa.q: What does Sumit staying by the tank suggest about him?
qa.a: It suggests Sumit was curious and troubled, and wanted to understand death rather than move on like the others.

qa.q: What did the teacher do next that respected Sumit's questions?
qa.a: They answered simply and honestly instead of brushing it off, held a small burial, and told his mother so she could continue the talk at home.

qa.q: How does Arnab see Sumit's questions?
qa.a: Arnab thinks they are silly because to him it was 'just a fish'.

grounding: Shows a child asking why things die and what happens next, and a teacher answering honestly and simply.

passage:
Monday night, in bed with the torch.
Dear Diary, today I asked Ritu Masi the biggest question. We were shelling peas on the balcony and I said, "Masi, why are we here? Like, why are there people at all?"
She didn't laugh or say "eat your peas." She put the bowl down. She said, "Honestly, Bhavna, nobody knows for sure. Some people think God made us for a reason. Some think we just happened. I think we're here to look after each other and notice nice things, like these peas."
Then I asked what happens after we die. She said she doesn't know that either, and that people have wondered about it for thousands of years.
I felt kind of grown-up that she told me the truth. I'm going to keep asking her things.

qa.q: What were Bhavna and Ritu Masi doing on the balcony?
qa.a: They were shelling peas on the balcony.

qa.q: How did Bhavna feel when Ritu Masi answered honestly?
qa.a: Bhavna felt kind of grown-up and trusted, pleased to be told the truth instead of being brushed off.

qa.q: What did Ritu Masi's way of answering get right?
qa.a: She stopped what she was doing, gave simple honest views, and admitted what nobody knows, which respected Bhavna's big question.

qa.q: What would change if Ritu Masi had said 'eat your peas'?
qa.a: Bhavna might have felt silly for asking and stopped bringing big questions to Masi.

grounding: Shows a child asking why people exist and what happens after death, and an adult answering simply and honestly instead of deflecting.

passage: In Kumbakonam, Keerthana's family couldn't keep up with her. In June she joined the temple choir and practised at dawn. By August she'd quit and started a plastic-free club with three classmates, marching through the bazaar with cloth bags. In October she painted the backyard wall with a huge peacock and talked for a week about becoming an artist. "Next month it'll be something else," her brother Ujjwal said at dinner, rolling his eyes. Keerthana put down her spoon. "At least I'm looking." That night Ujjwal found her on the terrace with her notebook. On one page she had written: "Things that make me feel alive: singing with others, the club, painting the peacock." Under it: "Maybe it's making things with people." She looked up. "It's not random, anna. I'm trying to figure it out."

qa.q: What did Keerthana paint on the backyard wall?
qa.a: A huge peacock.

qa.q: What was Keerthana feeling when she said 'At least I'm looking'?
qa.a: She felt hurt and defensive at Ujjwal's teasing, because her search mattered deeply to her even if it looked random.

qa.q: How could Ujjwal support Keerthana's search?
qa.a: He could ask her what she liked about each thing, instead of predicting she'll quit, and maybe join her on the next one.

qa.q: How does Ujjwal see Keerthana's changes at first?
qa.a: At first he sees them as random phases, rolling his eyes, until the notebook shows him she's taking it seriously.

passage: In Cape Town, Daniel's bedroom looked like three different people lived in it. There was a church youth group badge pinned to his curtain, a stack of vegan cookbooks from the library, and a borrowed bass guitar he was learning for a punk band. His mother called it "the Daniel museum." In one term he'd gone to Sunday services, then a climate march, then a poetry night. On Friday he told his friend Thabo, "I'm not trying to be cool. I just want to find the thing I'd get up at five in the morning for." Thabo laughed, then stopped when he saw Daniel's face. "Okay. So what's close?" Daniel thought. "The march. People who actually care." Thabo nodded. "Then maybe it's not the thing. Maybe it's the people."

qa.q: What did Daniel's mother call his bedroom?
qa.a: She called it 'the Daniel museum'.

qa.q: What does Daniel's face suggest when Thabo laughs?
qa.a: It suggests Daniel felt serious and a bit hurt, because this search matters deeply to him and isn't a joke.

qa.q: How did Thabo help once he stopped laughing?
qa.a: He asked what felt closest, which helped Daniel notice what he truly valued: people who actually care.

qa.a: She seems to find them a bit chaotic and amusing, calling the room a museum, without seeing how serious the search is inside.

passage: At the community centre library in Mysuru, Sangeeta spread out four forms on the table: debate club, animal shelter volunteers, a Sanskrit reading circle, and a street theatre group. Ira, the librarian's daughter and her closest friend, sat opposite with a samosa. "Last month you were going to be a lawyer," Ira said. "I know." "The month before, a vet." "I know." Sangeeta stared at the forms. "I'm not bored, Ira. I'm scared I'll pick wrong and spend my life on something that doesn't matter." Ira stopped chewing. "So try two. One for your head, one for your heart." Sangeeta picked up the shelter form and the theatre form. Then she looked at the Sanskrit circle again, and slipped it into her bag too, just in case.

qa.q: How many forms did Sangeeta spread out on the table?
qa.a: Four forms.

qa.q: What was Sangeeta worried about?
qa.a: She was scared she would pick wrong and spend her life on something that doesn't matter.

qa.q: What small step did Ira suggest, and why is it helpful?
qa.a: Trying two things, one for the head and one for the heart, keeps the search going without Sangeeta having to decide everything at once.

qa.q: How does Ira see Sangeeta's changing plans at first?
qa.a: At first Ira teases her about wanting to be a lawyer and then a vet, until Sangeeta explains how serious it feels.

grounding: Shows a teenager exploring causes, faith and art to find what feels worth living for, a search that is serious even if it looks chaotic.
